name: Oral probiotics (BLIS K12)

lead: Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 lozenges are meant to seed the mouth with friendly bacteria that compete with harmful ones. Breath-focused users take them hoping to reduce odor-producing species and get fresher breath.

The K12 strain of Streptococcus salivarius produces bacteriocin-like substances that can inhibit other bacteria, including strep throat bacteria. Lozenges are sold to support defence against more virulent streptococci. Breath-specific human evidence consists of a few small or registered trials, with no large published confirmation.

paras: They are dissolving lozenges, commonly taken after brushing so the strain can settle in the mouth, and often used after an antiseptic rinse. People generally use them over a stretch of days to weeks.
S. salivarius is usually harmless but is a rare opportunistic pathogen in people with very low white blood cell counts.

social.title: A scientific review of the clinical efficacy of oral probiotics

angle.text: BLIS K12 lozenges are taken for fresher breath by shifting the mouth's bacterial balance toward friendly strains and away from odor producers. Human data specific to breath is limited to a few small trials.

lead: Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 are lozenges or tablets containing live bacteria meant to settle in the mouth and throat. BLIS K12 contains Streptococcus salivarius K12, a strain that produces bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances (BLIS) that can hold back other bacteria.[1] People who use them for their looks are mostly after fresher breath: the idea is that a friendly bacterial population on the tongue and throat crowds out the species that produce smelly sulfur compounds, which makes close conversation and smiling more comfortable.

S. salivarius is one of the first bacteria to colonize the mouth and upper airway, and Wikipedia describes lozenges containing it being sold to support defence against more virulent streptococci, with some strains being trialed to prevent oral infections.[1] A registered trial in 120 orthodontic patients has examined oral probiotics for oral hygiene and halitosis,[2] and a published human trial has looked at the immune response to ingesting BLIS K12.[3] Published halitosis trials of K12 report mixed or modest results, with the largest effects described when the tongue coating is cleaned as well.

paras: S. salivarius is an early colonizer of the mouth and upper airway and is usually harmless, though it is an opportunistic pathogen that rarely enters the bloodstream in people with neutropenia.[1] BLIS-producing strains can inhibit other bacteria, including Streptococcus pyogenes, the cause of strep throat.[1]

K12 was first developed for throat health; breath freshness became a second common use because oral bacteria on the back of the tongue are the main source of volatile sulfur compounds. Products are sold as dissolving lozenges and tablets, typically taken after brushing.

For appearance, K12 sits alongside tongue scraping, flossing and mouthwash in breath routines. Proponents describe it as a way to maintain a favorable bacterial population after cleaning, rather than only removing bacteria.

Several small trials have compared K12 with placebo or with tongue cleaning for halitosis. Reported results vary: some describe lower odor scores and volatile sulfur compound levels for the first day or so, while others find the clearest improvement when probiotics are combined with tongue brushing or other cleaning.

A registered randomized trial of 120 orthodontic patients examined the effect of oral probiotics on oral hygiene and halitosis; it is listed as completed, with no results summarized in the registry record.[2] A registered trial in nursery-age children examined S. salivarius K12 for preventing upper respiratory tract infection. A randomized trial published in Probiotics and Antimicrobial Proteins in 2021 examined the human systemic immune response to ingesting BLIS K12.[3] A registered trial in 80 children has also examined probiotics and oral health.[4]

Published halitosis trials of K12 in adults and children have reported mixed results, with larger and more sustained improvements described when probiotic use was combined with tongue brushing or other mechanical cleaning. Many other oral-probiotic trials concern unrelated conditions such as infant gut disease or urinary infections.

S. salivarius is generally a harmless member of the mouth flora, but it is a rare opportunistic pathogen that can enter the bloodstream in people with very low neutrophil counts.[1] Reviews of other probiotic genera note that bloodstream infections are uncommon but carry higher risk in people with severe underlying disease.[5]
